papers.t: Pregnancy and classic Hodgkin lymphoma: real world outcomes from a single center in Egypt
papers.c: Management of CHL during pregnancy is a real challenge and requires a multidisciplinary approach with the goal of maximizing the cure rate for the patient, minimizing the fetal risks and allowing delivery of a healthy newborn. ABVD remains safe and effective in pregnancy, with excellent maternal and fetal outcomes.
ab: Background

Association of pregnancy and Classic Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL) is rare, but clinically important scenario because the peak incidence of CHL overlaps with reproductive years. Management requires balancing maternal disease control with fetal safety. This article aims to explore the clinicopathological characteristics, management challenges, and survival outcomes of CHL female patients in relation to pregnancy.
Patients And Methods

This is a retrospective study analyzed forty-one female patients in their childbearing period diagnosed with de novo or relapsed/refractory CHL that occurred during pregnancy and treated between 2010 and 2024.
Results And Outcomes

Mean age at diagnosis was 25.2 years (SD; 4.9). Thirty-nine patients received ABVD, two received BEACOPP. Complete remission was achieved in 75.6% of patients, with relapse in 6.5%. Median overall survival (OS) for the cohort was 95.33 months (range, 7.1-199.7). Pregnancy outcomes were favorable; most patients delivered full-term infants with no reported congenital anomalies. It appears that CHL and its treatment did not affect fertility and pregnancy itself did not worsen the lymphoma outcomes.
Conclusion

Management of CHL during pregnancy is a real challenge and requires a multidisciplinary approach with the goal of maximizing the cure rate for the patient, minimizing the fetal risks and allowing delivery of a healthy newborn. ABVD remains safe and effective in pregnancy, with excellent maternal and fetal outcomes.

papers.t: Hematological trajectories and pregnancy complications in essential thrombocythemia and polycythemia vera
papers.c: ET women who developed preeclampsia had significantly higher platelet counts before pregnancy and experienced a greater decline in platelet counts during pregnancy than women without preeclampsia. Thus, hematologic trajectories during pregnancy may help identify women at increased risk of preeclampsia.
ab: Women with essential thrombocythemia (ET) and polycythemia vera (PV) are at increased risk of pregnancy complications. During pregnancy, hematologic parameters tend to approach normal values, and previous studies have reported that a greater decline in platelet counts in ET is associated with reduced risk of complications. In this study, we examined longitudinal trajectories of platelet count, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and leukocyte count during pregnancy, characterized pregnancy outcomes, and investigated the association between platelet trajectories and preeclampsia. We established a longitudinal cohort of pregnant women with ET and PV in the Capital Region and Region Zealand between 2010 and 2024, using data from regional laboratory information systems and Danish health registries. In total, 41 ET and 5 PV pregnancies in 35 women were included. The mean age at MPN diagnosis was 30.1 years in women with ET and 34.1 years in women with PV. In ET pregnancies, platelet counts, hemoglobin, hematocrit and leukocyte count changed by - 44%, - 5%, - 12% and + 55%, respectively, from baseline to delivery, and in PV pregnancies - 36%, - 26%, - 25% and + 47%, respectively. Overall, 29% of ET pregnancies had a maternal complication, with preeclampsia being the most common (12%). ET women who developed preeclampsia had significantly higher platelet counts before pregnancy and experienced a greater decline in platelet counts during pregnancy than women without preeclampsia. Thus, hematologic trajectories during pregnancy may help identify women at increased risk of preeclampsia.

papers.t: Gemtuzumab Ozogamicin for Patients with Newly Diagnosed CD33-Positive Acute Myeloid Leukemia: A French Retrospective Observational Study
papers.c: Results demonstrate real-world safety and clinical outcomes of GO plus induction therapy for patients with de novo CD33-positive AML.
ab: Introduction

Gemtuzumab ozogamicin (GO), a CD33-targeted antibody-drug conjugate, is approved in combination with daunorubicin/cytarabine for patients ≥ 15 years with de novo, CD33-positive acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
Methods

This retrospective, observational study assessed real-world use, clinical outcomes, and safety of GO in 113 patients with de novo AML treated between 2014 and 2022 in the French authorization for temporary use (ATU) and post-ATU program.
Results

During first induction, most patients (98.1%; 105/107) received GO with other agents, mainly daunorubicin/cytarabine (60.0%; 63/105). After 44.6 months' median follow-up (95% CI: 33.8-69.3), 78.6% (88/112) responded; 72.3% (81/112) achieved complete response, 52.2% (24/46) without measurable residual disease. Median (95% CI) event-free survival (EFS), relapse-free survival (RFS), and overall survival (OS) were 13.1 months (9.9-17.5), 17.5 months (12.6-35.6), and 49.8 months (21.8-not estimable), respectively. Overall, 46.9% of patients died. Older age predicted shorter OS (p < 0.001). FLT3-TKD mutation (p = 0.013) and adverse cytogenetic classification (p = 0.015) predicted shorter EFS. ECOG performance status ≥ 2 (p = 0.005) and adverse cytogenetic classification (p = 0.001) predicted shorter RFS. Forty-four patients (38.9%) reported ≥ 1 adverse event of interest; 13.3% were serious and 26.6% treatment-related; most commonly thrombocytopenia (21.2%). GO was predominantly administered per indication. No new safety signals were reported.
Conclusions
Results demonstrate real-world safety and clinical outcomes of GO plus induction therapy for patients with de novo CD33-positive AML.
Trial Registration
EU Post Authorization Study (PAS) register number: EUPAS44551.

papers.t: Acute myeloid leukemia with TP53 mutation: molecular mechanisms and therapeutic advances
papers.c: Recent studies indicate that the biological effects of TP53 abnormalities depend not only on the mutation itself but also on allelic status, clonal evolution, cytogenetic background, and the immune and metabolic microenvironments. This review summarizes the molecular features, clonal evolution, immune microenvironment, and metabolic reprogramming of TP53-mutated AML; its biological mechanisms, prognostic implications, and therapeutic advances; and the major challenges of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and novel therapeutic strategies.
ab: TP53-mutated acute myeloid leukemia (AML) accounts for approximately 5%-10% of newly diagnosed AML. It is characterized by enrichment of complex karyotypes, genomic instability, and treatment resistance, resulting in an extremely poor overall prognosis. Although intensive chemotherapy and hypomethylating agents (HMAs) combined with venetoclax can induce remission in some patients, remission duration and long-term survival remain unsatisfactory; novel treatments targeting the p53 pathway, immune microenvironment, and metabolic vulnerabilities have likewise not achieved a breakthrough. Recent studies indicate that the biological effects of TP53 abnormalities depend not only on the mutation itself but also on allelic status, clonal evolution, cytogenetic background, and the immune and metabolic microenvironments. This review summarizes the molecular features, clonal evolution, immune microenvironment, and metabolic reprogramming of TP53-mutated AML; its biological mechanisms, prognostic implications, and therapeutic advances; and the major challenges of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and novel therapeutic strategies.

papers.t: Low-dose 10-day decitabine plus venetoclax induced rapid MRD negativity and durable remission in De Novo AML
papers.c: The multivariate analysis showed that patients with ECOG < 3 and non-complex karyotype had significantly better OS. The regimen of low-dose 10-day DEC plus VEN induced rapid MRD negativity with good tolerability, along with high long-term survival in patient ineligible for intensive therapy.
ab: The combination of hypomethylating agents and venetoclax (VEN) has emerged as a new standard of care for elderly or unfit patients. In this study, we conducted a retrospective analysis of 37 patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) to investigate the efficacy and safety of a low‑dose 10‑day decitabine (DEC) combined with venetoclax (VEN) regimen (DEC 6 mg/m2 for 10 days and VEN for 14 days). The composite complete remission (CRc) rate was 78.4%, with 88.9% in favorable group and 75.0% in intermediate/adverse group according to ELN-2022 risk stratification. Among patients who achieved CRc, 79.3% patients attained MRD negativity after the first cycle. With a median follow-up of 40.0 months, the median overall survival (OS) was 36.1 months. The 36-month OS and EFS rates were 35.0% and 40.4%. Hematologic toxicities were the most common adverse events. The multivariate analysis showed that patients with ECOG < 3 and non-complex karyotype had significantly better OS. The regimen of low-dose 10-day DEC plus VEN induced rapid MRD negativity with good tolerability, along with high long-term survival in patient ineligible for intensive therapy.

papers.t: Optimizing Reduced-Intensity Conditioning for Older Patients with AML and MDS: A Large-Scale Analysis from the CIBMTR
papers.c: In conclusion, FM100 and FM140 provide superior long-term survival and DFS for older patients with AML/MDS by providing potent anti-leukemic activity that offsets higher early toxicity. These findings support FM-based RIC as the preferred conditioning platform for this population, regardless of baseline comorbidities.
ab: The optimal reduced-intensity conditioning (RIC) regimen for older patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (AHCT) remains undefined. We utilized CIBMTR registry data (2013-2022) to compare five common fludarabine-based regimens in 11,731 patients aged ≥50 years: fludarabine combined with 2 days of busulfan (FB2), melphalan 100 mg/m² (FM100), melphalan 140 mg/m² (FM140), or 2 Gy TBI with (FCT) or without (FT) cyclophosphamide. Using propensity score inverse probability weighting and Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART), we found that Fludarabine-melphalan (FM) regimens demonstrated superior long-term survival. Although FM140, FCT, and FT showed higher early mortality (≤6 months) than FB2 (P=.036), both FM100 (HR 0.79) and FM140 (HR 0.77) achieved significantly better late (> 6 months) overall survival (OS), outperforming all other regimens (P<.0001). In the 2019-2022 cohort, FM100, FM140, and FCT provided improved disease-free survival (DFS) relative to FB2. Specifically, FM100 yielded superior DFS compared to FCT (P=0.002) and FT (P=0.007). FM-based conditioning consistently resulted in lower relapse rates (P<.0001) and improved late GVHD-free/relapse-free survival. While FM regimens faced higher early non-relapse mortality (NRM), this impact did not persist beyond 6 months. BART analysis confirmed that these survival and relapse benefits remained robust across various patient comorbidities. In conclusion, FM100 and FM140 provide superior long-term survival and DFS for older patients with AML/MDS by providing potent anti-leukemic activity that offsets higher early toxicity. These findings support FM-based RIC as the preferred conditioning platform for this population, regardless of baseline comorbidities.

papers.t: Aligning Clinical Trial Reporting: A systematic analysis and position statement by the International Consortium for MDS
papers.c: Informed by the results of this analysis, we then performed a modified-Delphi process for members of the International Consortium for MDS (icMDS) to develop consensus-based recommendations for consistent and accurate reporting of MDS clinical trial results. We advocate that these recommendations serve as benchmarks and templates for clinical trial reporting in MDS to improve interpretability and comparison of results.
ab: Variability in how clinical trial elements are reported can hinder accurate interpretation and comparison of trial results. Here, we systematically analyzed published manuscripts of therapeutic clinical trials in myelodysplastic syndromes/neoplasms (MDS) focusing on how key data elements were reported and made recommendations on how to improve this reporting. We included peer-reviewed full text manuscripts that reported results of clinical trials in MDS and were published between January 1, 2015 to December 31, 2024. We analyzed the presence or absence of several pre-determined key reporting elements and then synthesized these data to evaluate for consistency across manuscripts. We identified substantial variability in descriptions of patient characteristics, as well as the definitions used for response criteria. For example, baseline ANC was reported in only 16% of lower-risk MDS studies and 23% of higher-risk MDS studies, while baseline bone marrow blast percentage was reported in only 55% of higher-risk MDS manuscripts. In addition, response endpoints lacked standardization, with six unique definitions of RBC transfusion independence identified in lower-risk MDS trials and seven different definitions of overall response rate identified in higher-risk MDS trials. Informed by the results of this analysis, we then performed a modified-Delphi process for members of the International Consortium for MDS (icMDS) to develop consensus-based recommendations for consistent and accurate reporting of MDS clinical trial results. We advocate that these recommendations serve as benchmarks and templates for clinical trial reporting in MDS to improve interpretability and comparison of results.

papers.t: Disease biology rather than donor type determines transplant outcomes in KMT2A-rearranged AML
papers.c: In KMT2A-r AML undergoing allo-HSCT in complete remission, post-transplant outcome is determined predominantly by leukemia biology rather than donor platform. These findings support a shift from donor-centered transplantation toward biology-driven risk assessment and individualized post-transplant management.
ab: The relative contributions of donor selection and disease biology to transplant outcomes in KMT2A-rearranged (KMT2A-r) acute myeloid leukemia (AML) remain poorly defined. We retrospectively analyzed 241 consecutive patients with KMT2A-r AML undergoing first allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) in complete remission (192 HID, 29 MSD, 20 MUD). We evaluated the impact of donor type, fusion partners, cooperating mutations, pre-transplant measurable residual disease (MRD), and disease status on post-transplant outcomes. After a median follow-up of 28.4 months, the estimated 2-year overall survival (OS), leukemia-free survival (LFS), cumulative incidence of relapse (CIR), and non-relapse mortality (NRM) were 80.0%, 78.9%, 9.5%, and 14.3%, respectively. Post-transplant outcomes were comparable across donor platforms. Likewise, transplant outcomes did not differ among major KMT2A fusion partners. In contrast, disease-related factors independently predicted prognosis. NRAS mutation remained independently associated with inferior OS (HR 2.70, P = 0.003) and LFS (HR 2.37, P = 0.008). Compared with transplantation in CR1, transplantation in ≥CR2 independently predicted worse OS (HR 2.71, P = 0.005), LFS (HR 2.40, P = 0.012), and higher NRM (HR 3.17, P = 0.006). Pre-transplant concurrent positivity by both MFC and RT-qPCR for KMT2A fusion transcripts (MFC+/RT-qPCR+) was the strongest adverse prognostic factor, independently predicting inferior survival and increased relapse, while isolated molecular positivity (MFC-/RT-qPCR+) also remained associated with inferior OS and LFS. An exploratory biologic risk stratification integrating NRAS mutation, transplantation in ≥CR2, and molecular MRD positivity effectively identified patients at high risk of treatment failure, with 2-year OS of 50.4% versus 85.6% and LFS of 48.6% versus 84.6% (both P < 0.0001). In KMT2A-r AML undergoing allo-HSCT in complete remission, post-transplant outcome is determined predominantly by leukemia biology rather than donor platform. These findings support a shift from donor-centered transplantation toward biology-driven risk assessment and individualized post-transplant management.

papers.t: Allogeneic CD33/CD123 CAR-T сells in pediatric relapsed/refractory AML: early single-center experience
Modulation of the RNA-sensing RIG/MAVS pathway bypasses resistance to hypomethylating agents in acute myeloid leukemia
papers.c: Treatment with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) restored RIG-I pathway activity and antileukemic response in mice bearing HMA-resistant AML. Our findings not only delineate a critical link between epigenetic modulation and innate immune activation in AML but also provide a rationale for targeting the RIG-I/MAVS RNA-sensing pathway to enhance antileukemic immunity and bypass epigenetic resistance to HMA.
ab: DNA hypomethylating agents (HMAs) such as 5-azacytidine (5-AZA) are a cornerstone in the treatment of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but development of resistance represents a major clinical challenge. Apart from epigenetic reprogramming of malignant cell clones, therapy with HMA is increasingly recognized to facilitate antineoplastic immunity, yet the relevance of these molecular mechanisms in AML remains poorly defined. Here, we show that AML cell-intrinsic sensing of aberrant RNA via the innate receptor system retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)/mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS) is essential for the therapeutic activity of HMAs. In human and murine AML cell lines, HMA treatment induced robust RIG-I/MAVS pathway activation and subsequent Type I interferon (IFN-I) release. HMA enhanced transcriptional activity of endogenous retroviral (ERV) elements that readily bound to the RIG-I receptor. Analysis of a small series of patient samples linked treatment response to elevated gene expression of ERV and RIG-I/MAVS pathway components in CD34+ cells including AML blasts. AML-intrinsic genetic ablation of MAVS or RIG-I abrogated the HMA treatment effects in mice by interfering with host IFN-I signaling and subsequent expansion and accumulation of activated T cells. Acquired HMA resistance was associated with ERV suppression and blunted RIG-I/MAVS signaling. Treatment with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) restored RIG-I pathway activity and antileukemic response in mice bearing HMA-resistant AML. Our findings not only delineate a critical link between epigenetic modulation and innate immune activation in AML but also provide a rationale for targeting the RIG-I/MAVS RNA-sensing pathway to enhance antileukemic immunity and bypass epigenetic resistance to HMA.

papers.t: Teclistamab in multiple myeloma with coexisting myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia
Mediator kinase inhibition exposes a transcriptional vulnerability and synergizes with venetoclax in AML
papers.c: Notably, CDK8 inhibition synergized with venetoclax in AML cell lines and patient-derived xenograft models, resulting in enhanced anti-leukemic activity in vivo. Collectively, these findings establish CDK8/CDK19 inhibition as a therapeutically relevant strategy in AML.
ab: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a heterogeneous and aggressive hematologic malignancy associated with poor survival despite recent therapeutic advances. To identify novel anti-leukemic agents, we performed a high-throughput viability screen of 10,000 small molecules across 56 genetically diverse primary AML samples. Compounds with similar activity profiles were grouped into Compound Correlation Clusters (CCCs), leading to the identification of CCC163, which includes AML874, as a potent and selective hit. Integrated pharmacological and CRISPR-Cas9 approaches identified the Mediator complex as the molecular target of AML874. We demonstrated that AML874 acts as a selective CDK8/CDK19 inhibitor, disrupting Mediator-dependent transcription. FLT3-mutated AML showed increased sensitivity to AML874, suggesting a subtype-specific vulnerability. Notably, CDK8 inhibition synergized with venetoclax in AML cell lines and patient-derived xenograft models, resulting in enhanced anti-leukemic activity in vivo. Collectively, these findings establish CDK8/CDK19 inhibition as a therapeutically relevant strategy in AML.

papers.t: NPM1-mutated AML: One entity, multiple layers of heterogeneity
papers.c: Rare variants of NPM1 mutations share a similar molecular background to the common NPM1 type A variant and are associated with similar survival in adults with acute myeloid leukaemia. Br J Haematol 2026 (Online ahead of print). doi: 10.1182/blood-2024-202884.
ab: Nucleophosmin 1 (NPM1) mutations are found in around one third of all acute myeloid leukaemias (AMLs). However, little is known about the clinical role of the rare, non-A NPM1 variants. Sangiorgio et al. showed that rare variants shared a similar molecular background and overall survival to the common type A, with FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3) status as the main determinant of outcome. Commentary on: Sangiorgio et al. Rare variants of NPM1 mutations share a similar molecular background to the common NPM1 type A variant and are associated with similar survival in adults with acute myeloid leukaemia. Br J Haematol 2026 (Online ahead of print). doi: 10.1182/blood-2024-202884.

papers.t: Rare variants of NPM1 mutations share a similar molecular background to the common NPM1 type A variant and are associated with similar survival in adults with acute myeloid leukaemia
MicroRNA dysregulation in mesenchymal stromal cells in myelodysplastic syndromes and its modulation by azacitidine and bortezomib
papers.c: Functional enrichment analyses linked dysregulated miRNAs to extracellular matrix organization, inflammatory signaling and epigenetic regulation, supporting their role in MSC dysfunction. These findings identify stromal miRNAs as potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets in MDS.
ab: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are clonal disorders of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis, bone marrow dysplasia and variable progression to acute myeloid leukemia. Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) contribute to MDS pathogenesis through mechanisms partly mediated by microRNAs (miRNAs). We characterized the miRNA profile of MDS-derived MSCs and evaluated its modulation by 5-azacitidine (5-AZA) and bortezomib (BTZ). Small RNA sequencing and RT-qPCR identified significant downregulation of miR-20a-5p in MDS-MSCs, while 5-AZA restored its expression to control levels. Reduced miR-20a-5p was also detected in plasma from MDS patients, supporting its biomarker potential. BTZ induced a marked 5-6-fold upregulation of miR-192-5p in patient- and control-derived MSCs. Functional enrichment analyses linked dysregulated miRNAs to extracellular matrix organization, inflammatory signaling and epigenetic regulation, supporting their role in MSC dysfunction. These findings identify stromal miRNAs as potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets in MDS.

papers.t: BCR::ABL1 emergence during menin inhibitor therapy in two patients with relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia
Advances in CBFA2T3::GLIS2 fusion gene in pediatric acute myeloid leukemia: from molecular mechanisms to targeted therapeutic strategies
papers.c: However, the molecular mechanisms underlying C/G fusion-driven leukemogenesis remain incompletely characterized. This review provides an overview of the pathogenic mechanisms, emerging therapeutic strategies, and clinical challenges associated with C/G-positive pediatric AML.
ab: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a genetically heterogeneous hematologic malignancy in children, with molecular alterations playing critical roles in disease development and therapeutic responses. The CBFA2T3::GLIS2 (C/G) is the most frequent genetic alteration identified in non-Down syndrome acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL) and results from a cryptic inversion involving the subtelomeric region of chromosome 16. Multiple chimeric transcripts can be generated depending on the breakpoint location, with CBFA2T3-ex11/GLIS2-ex3 being the predominant transcript. This fusion gene is associated with chemotherapy resistance and an unfavorable clinical outcome. Although initially identified in AMKL, it has also been detected in several cytogenetically normal AML subtypes, including M0, M1, M2, M4, and M5. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying C/G fusion-driven leukemogenesis remain incompletely characterized. This review provides an overview of the pathogenic mechanisms, emerging therapeutic strategies, and clinical challenges associated with C/G-positive pediatric AML.

papers.t: Mesenchymal stromal cells drive immune escape in MDS and sAML through metabolic rewiring of NK cells
papers.c: Together, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized loss of supportive capacity in pathological MSCs that hampers NK-cell fitness. Therapeutic approaches that bolster mitochondrial resilience in NK cells may help counteract this microenvironment-induced impairment and strengthen immune surveillance in MDS and sAML.
ab: Myelodysplastic neoplasms (MDS) are clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorders that frequently progress to secondary acute myeloid leukemia (sAML). Besides intrinsic genetic changes, the disease's development is heavily influenced by the bone marrow (BM) microenvironment, especially mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs). In this study, we present a comprehensive characterization of how unhealthy MSCs affect natural killer (NK) cell anti-leukemic function in MDS and sAML. Using integrated ATAC-seq and RNA-seq profiling, we show that MDS/sAML-derived MSCs induce profound chromatin remodeling in NK cells, marked by reduced promoter accessibility and downregulation of genes essential for stress response and survival. Functionally, pathological MSCs fail to deliver the protective support normally provided by healthy MSCs, instead driving mitochondrial fragmentation and apoptosis in NK cells, ultimately suppressing their cytotoxic activity. Together, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized loss of supportive capacity in pathological MSCs that hampers NK-cell fitness. Therapeutic approaches that bolster mitochondrial resilience in NK cells may help counteract this microenvironment-induced impairment and strengthen immune surveillance in MDS and sAML.

papers.t: Safety and feasibility of peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) placement in patients with newly diagnosed acute leukemia: A single-center retrospective study
papers.c: The technique was safe and feasible, and PLT and Fg helped predict bleeding risk. Prospective multicenter validation is warranted.
ab: Patients with newly diagnosed acute leukemia are at increased risk of bleeding during vascular access because of thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy. The primary objective of this single-center retrospective study (November 2023-August 2024; Ruijin Hospital) was to evaluate the feasibility and safety of a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) puncture and nursing protocol incorporating ultrasound-guided Seldinger puncture, controlled sheath withdrawal with gauze-assisted compression, and localized hemostatic dressing in 101 patients prior to chemotherapy. The first-attempt success rate was 95.1%. At 24 h, active oozing occurred in 14 patients (13.9%); all events were CTCAE grade 1-2 and were controlled with local measures. Platelet count (PLT; OR = 0.972, P = 0.029) and fibrinogen (Fg; OR = 0.594, P = 0.049) were independent predictors of bleeding. On ROC analysis, PLT showed greater predictive value (AUC = 0.762, 95% CI 0.628-0.880). Catheter malposition and thrombosis each occurred in 1.0% of patients (CTCAE grade 2 and grade 1, respectively); no phlebitis, catheter-related infection, or grade ≥ 3 adverse events were reported. The technique was safe and feasible, and PLT and Fg helped predict bleeding risk. Prospective multicenter validation is warranted.

papers.t: Real-world access and barriers to CAR T-cell therapy in relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: a population-based study
papers.c: A publicly funded provincial CAR-T program enabled approximately two-thirds of patients initiating 2L or 3L+ therapy for R/R DLBCL to access CAR-T with favorable real-world outcomes. Poor fitness and uncontrolled disease, rather than geographic or social factors, were the dominant barriers. Novel strategies are urgently needed for the minority of patients who do not receive CAR-T.
ab: Background

CAR T-cell therapy has transformed outcomes of relapsed/refractory (R/R) diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), but access may be limited by clinical, geographic, logistical, and socioeconomic constraints. While <30% of eligible patients in the United States are estimated to receive CAR-T, little is known about population-level utilization and barriers to CAR-T within publicly funded healthcare systems such as Canada.
Objectives
To determine the proportion of patients with R/R DLBCL who were intended for and treated with CAR-T, to identify barriers to treatment, and to describe clinical outcomes.
Study Design

This retrospective, population-based study included all adults diagnosed with DLBCL in 2023 and 2024 in the province of Alberta, Canada who subsequently initiated third-line or later (3L+) therapy at any time, or second-line therapy (2L) within 12 months of first-line treatment as of the approval of 2L CAR-T in November 2024. During this period, CAR-T was publicly funded through provincial health insurance and delivered at two referral centers in Calgary and Edmonton, serving a province of nearly 5 million people across 640,000 km². Patient support programs were available to reimburse travel expenses.
Results

The study population comprised 93 patients who initiated 2L (n=51) or 3L+ (n=42) therapy for R/R DLBCL. Median age was 67 years (range 22-89), 67% were male, and 77% were married. Most (91%) lived in urban settings, with 23% residing >100km from a CAR-T center. In total, 67 (72%) patients were documented to be intended for CAR-T, of whom 65 (97%) underwent leukapheresis and 62 (93%) completed infusion. Failure to reach infusion was due to uncontrolled lymphoma (n=4) or patient decision (n=1). Objective response and complete response rates to CAR-T were 77% and 50%, respectively. Twelve-month progression-free survival (PFS) was 56% (95% CI 43-67%) and overall survival (OS) was 81% (95% CI 68-89%) among patients intended for CAR-T. There were 26 (28%) patients not intended for CAR-T due to uncontrolled lymphoma (n=12), advanced age/frailty (n=10), poor performance status (n=9), comorbidities (n=7), toxicity concerns (n=5), patient preference (n=4), unresolved complications from prior therapy (n=3), and/or psychosocial reasons (n=1). Geographic distance and marital status were not documented as barriers. Compared to those intended for CAR-T, these patients were older (median age 74 versus 64, p<0.0001) and more likely to have ECOG >1 (62% versus 25%, p=0.0016) and IPI score 3-5 (73% versus 48%, p=0.037). Non-CAR-T therapies included chemoimmunotherapy (n=10), an antibody-drug conjugate-based regimen (n=7), radiation (n=5), or bispecific antibodies (n=4). Twelve-month PFS and OS were 25% (95% CI 9-44%) and 30% (95% CI 11-51%), respectively.
Conclusions

A publicly funded provincial CAR-T program enabled approximately two-thirds of patients initiating 2L or 3L+ therapy for R/R DLBCL to access CAR-T with favorable real-world outcomes. Poor fitness and uncontrolled disease, rather than geographic or social factors, were the dominant barriers. Novel strategies are urgently needed for the minority of patients who do not receive CAR-T.

papers.t: Bridging to CD19 CAR T-cell therapy for large B-cell lymphoma: An analysis of 1,134 patients by the EBMT Lymphoma Working Party and the GoCART Coalition
papers.c: BT modality influenced conversion rates but not adjusted OS, PFS, or relapse. Our data suggest bridging therapy may prioritize disease control with minimal toxicity rather than any specific regimen.
ab: CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy (CAR T) is effective in relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma (R/R LBCL), but the role of bridging therapy (BT) remains incompletely defined. We analyzed 1,134 patients with R/R LBCL treated with axicabtagene ciloleucel or tisagenlecleucel between 2018 and July 2023. BT was categorized as polatuzumab vedotin-bendamustine-rituximab (Pola-BR), low-dose regimens, classical salvage chemo-immunotherapy, or radiotherapy. Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) from CAR T infusion were primary endpoints. Overall, 900 patients (79.5%) received BT and 232 (20.5%) did not (No-BT). At lymphodepletion, BT recipients more often had elevated LDH, bulky disease, and ECOG ≥2, yet had higher complete remission rates. Three-year PFS was 34.3% with BT versus 44.7% with No-BT, and OS was 44.4% versus 57.4%. In multivariable analyses, No-BT remained associated with superior OS (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.49-0.82) and PFS (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.55-0.87). Improvement in disease status between apheresis and lymphodepletion occurred more often with BT and was associated with improved outcomes (3-year PFS 47.5% vs. 28.9 and 27.7% for stable/worsened disease among BT recipients). BT modality influenced conversion rates but not adjusted OS, PFS, or relapse. Our data suggest bridging therapy may prioritize disease control with minimal toxicity rather than any specific regimen.

papers.t: Severe graft-versus-host disease and limited durable response with mogamulizumab for post-transplant relapse of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma
papers.c: MOG demonstrated clinically meaningful short-term antitumor activity in patients with post-transplant relapsed ATL, particularly in peripheral blood disease, but was associated with a substantial risk of severe acute GVHD and limited durable disease control. Careful patient selection and rational sequential or combination treatment strategies are warranted to optimize MOG use after allo-HCT.
ab: Background
The safety and efficacy of mogamulizumab (MOG) for post-transplant relapse of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL) remain uncertain.
Objectives
We investigated the clinical outcomes of MOG therapy, with particular attention to graft-versus-host disease and antitumor efficacy, in patients with post-transplant relapsed ATL.
Study Design
We retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients who received MOG for post-transplant relapsed ATL at a single center.
Results

Thirty-three consecutive patients received MOG for post-transplant relapsed ATL. The median interval from allo-HCT to MOG initiation was 104 days. The cumulative incidence of grade II-IV acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) by day 100 after MOG initiation was 55.8%, including grade III-IV acute GVHD in 34.2% of patients. Severe acute GVHD developed irrespective of the interval between transplantation and MOG initiation. Exploratory analyses identified unrelated peripheral blood stem cell transplantation and lower soluble interleukin-2 receptor levels at MOG initiation as factors associated with grade III-IV acute GVHD. The overall response rate was 61%, including complete remission in 39% of patients, with the highest response observed in peripheral blood disease. However, relapse or disease progression occurred in 15 of the 20 responders. The median overall survival (OS) from MOG initiation was 6.9 months, with 1- and 2-year OS rates of 40.6% and 21.9%, respectively.
Conclusions

MOG demonstrated clinically meaningful short-term antitumor activity in patients with post-transplant relapsed ATL, particularly in peripheral blood disease, but was associated with a substantial risk of severe acute GVHD and limited durable disease control. Careful patient selection and rational sequential or combination treatment strategies are warranted to optimize MOG use after allo-HCT.

papers.t: Second Cancer Risk in Female Survivors of Hodgkin Lymphoma: A National Cohort Analysis Across Treatment Eras
papers.c: Female patients treated in more recent eras have a substantially lower long-term risk of solid SPMs largely attributable to the reduced use, dose, and improvement in radiotherapy. Nevertheless, persistently elevated risks remained beyond 50 years of follow-up, particularly for lung and breast cancer, underscoring the need for lifelong surveillance and targeted screening of survivors.
ab: Purpose

Subsequent primary malignancies (SPMs) are the leading cause of long-term treatment-related mortality in Hodgkin lymphoma (HL). Although treatments have evolved substantially over recent decades, few studies have demonstrated reductions in SPM risks following modern treatments, nor how such changes should inform survivorship care and screening. We analyzed SPM risks in a large female cohort of childhood and adult patients with HL treated over a 60-year period.
Materials And Methods

This population-based cohort study included 7,428 women diagnosed with HL before age 36 years in England and Wales from 1954 to 2010, with follow-up through 2018. SPMs were ascertained via national cancer registry linkages. Standardized incidence ratios (SIRs), absolute excess risks, and multivariable models were used to assess temporal trends and associations with treatment.
Results

During a median follow-up of 20.2 years, 1,200 women developed 1,467 invasive cancers (SIR, 3.3 [95% CI, 3.1 to 3.5]), most commonly breast, lung, and thyroid cancers. Solid tumor risks were the highest following radiotherapy, with a strong dose-dependent response. Alkylator use with radiotherapy was associated with reduced risks of breast cancer but increased risks of GI cancers. Solid cancer risks decreased by 25% between treatment periods 1954-1989 and 2000-2010. The decrease was attenuated and nonsignificant after adjustment for radiotherapy but not affected by adjustment for chemotherapy. No decline was observed for hematologic malignancies. Cumulative incidence of SPMs reached 36% at 50 years.
Conclusion

Female patients treated in more recent eras have a substantially lower long-term risk of solid SPMs largely attributable to the reduced use, dose, and improvement in radiotherapy. Nevertheless, persistently elevated risks remained beyond 50 years of follow-up, particularly for lung and breast cancer, underscoring the need for lifelong surveillance and targeted screening of survivors.

papers.t: Response to comment on: "Immune checkpoint therapy in pediatric and adolescent lymphomas"
Transcriptional landscape of nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma and T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma: tumor microenvironment and checkpoint genes
papers.c: Signatures defined a spectrum from classic to variant NLPHL and THRLBCL. External validation in independent cohorts reproduced this gradient, supporting a continuous microenvironmental spectrum spanning NLPHL and THRLBCL.
ab: Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (NLPHL) is a rare B-cell malignancy with an indolent course, yet some cases relapse or transform to Tcell/ histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma (THRLBCL). Biological factors underlying poor outcomes in NLPHL are largely unknown, and the relationship between THRLBCL and untransformed NLPHL has not been systematically defined. We analyzed 178 NLPHL and 22 THRLBCL cases using whole-transcriptome RNA sequencing and clinical data. NLPHL patients were younger, had limited-stage disease, and better outcomes than THRLBCL patients. Variant immuno-architectural patterns (IAP) in NLPHL showed THRLBCL-like transcriptional profiles, especially with splenic involvement and high Lymphocyte-Predominant International Prognostic Score (LP-IPS). In-silico deconvolution of the tumor microenvironment (TME) revealed B-cell enrichment in classic NLPHL, intermediate profiles in variant NLPHL, and increased activated CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells and macrophages in THRLBCL. Higher follicular helper T-cell content was associated with shorter event-free survival in an exploratory analysis. NLPHL cases showed strong B-cell and T-helper signatures, whereas THRLBCL cases were enriched for macrophage and cytotoxic T-cell pathways and expressed higher immune checkpoint genes, suggesting an immunosuppressive TME. Signatures defined a spectrum from classic to variant NLPHL and THRLBCL. External validation in independent cohorts reproduced this gradient, supporting a continuous microenvironmental spectrum spanning NLPHL and THRLBCL.

papers.t: How Many Lines of Therapy Do Patients With Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia/Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma Receive in Routine Clinical Practice in the United States? Real World Evidence From the Targeted Therapy Era
papers.c: Alongside increasing adoption of targeted therapies in CLL/SLL, many patients may receive no more than two LoTs, underscoring the impact of early treatment decisions.
ab: Introduction

Historically, treatment-eligible patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) received sequential chemoimmunotherapy (CIT)-based regimens across multiple lines of therapy (LoTs). Shift to targeted therapies has improved survival; however, its impact on the number of LoTs received in the real-world remains uncharacterized.
Methods

This study analyzed adults diagnosed with CLL/SLL (2015-2023) receiving at least one CLL/SLL-directed therapy (first-line initiation = index) using US Flatiron Health Research Database. Baseline characteristics and treatments were described overall, by practice type and diagnosis eras (2015-2017, 2018-2020, 2021-2023). Multivariable logistic regression evaluated factors associated with receipt of 1-2 LoTs (vs. ≥ 3); odds ratio (OR; 95% confidence intervals [CIs]) were reported. Sensitivity analyses included landmark and time-to-event approaches, accounting for differential follow-up.
Results

Among 6898 patients, median (Q1-Q3) age at index was 71 years (63-78); 84% were treated in community settings. Overall, 88% patients received only 1-2 LoTs; this proportion ranged 83-95% across eras, with shorter follow-up in the 2021-2023 era. Most patients received targeted therapy in first-line (62%) and second-line (64%) with increasing use across eras and similar pattern across practice settings. Robust factors associated with higher odds of receiving 1-2 LoTs included first-line targeted therapy use (1.57 [1.27-1.94]) and longer time from diagnosis to index (1.09 [1.03-1.15]), whereas del(17p)/TP53-aberrant disease (0.60 [0.47-0.76]) was associated with lower odds.
Conclusion
Alongside increasing adoption of targeted therapies in CLL/SLL, many patients may receive no more than two LoTs, underscoring the impact of early treatment decisions.

papers.t: Thiotepa/Busulfan/Cyclophosphamide versus Busulfan/Thiotepa Conditioning For Autologous Stem Cell Transplantation in CNS Lymphoma: A Single-Center Comparative and Descriptive Experience
papers.c: In this comparison - including, to our knowledge, one of the largest reported BuTT cohorts to date - BuTT conditioning appeared to achieve similar early disease control to TBC in PCNSL patients in CR1 at short follow-up, with lower rates of severe mucositis and no non-relapse mortality, though current data cannot establish statistical equivalence and cannot exclude a late erosion of disease control with reduced-intensity conditioning. Larger, prospective, multi-center studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these findings and define BuTT's role beyond the CR1 setting.
ab: Background

Autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) with thiotepa-based conditioning improves outcomes in primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL), but standard thiotepa/busulfan/cyclophosphamide (TBC) conditioning is associated with substantial toxicity, particularly among older or less fit patients. Busulfan/thiotepa (BuTT) conditioning reduces busulfan and thiotepa dose intensity in addition to omitting cyclophosphamide, and has been proposed as a better-tolerated alternative, but comparative real-world data remain limited.
Objective(S)

To compare outcomes of TBC versus BuTT conditioning in patients with PCNSL in first complete remission (CR1) at the time of ASCT; outcomes among patients treated outside this CR1 consolidation setting are described in the Supplement.
Study Design

We retrospectively identified all adult patients undergoing ASCT for PCNSL or SCNSL at a single center (January 2010-January 2026). Cohort 1 comprised patients with PCNSL in CR1 who received TBC (n=18) or BuTT (n=18), analyzed comparatively; an additional 37 patients treated outside this CR1 setting are presented descriptively in the Supplement given their heterogeneity.
Results

In Cohort 1, BuTT recipients were significantly older (median 69 vs. 52 years), more often female, and had lower Karnofsky performance status than TBC recipients, consistent with an institutional practice of reserving BuTT for less fit patients since 2020. One- and 2-year overall survival were 94% (TBC) and 100% (BuTT); 1- and 2-year progression-free survival were 89% and 93%, respectively (log-rank p=NS for both). Grade 3-4 mucositis was less frequent with BuTT (28% vs. 72%) despite the expected direction of selection bias, and this difference persisted in a pooled institutional analysis of all patients treated with each regimen (32% vs. 78%, n=73). Both deaths in Cohort 1 were non-relapse mortality in TBC recipients; no BuTT recipients died.
Conclusion(S)

In this comparison - including, to our knowledge, one of the largest reported BuTT cohorts to date - BuTT conditioning appeared to achieve similar early disease control to TBC in PCNSL patients in CR1 at short follow-up, with lower rates of severe mucositis and no non-relapse mortality, though current data cannot establish statistical equivalence and cannot exclude a late erosion of disease control with reduced-intensity conditioning. Larger, prospective, multi-center studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm these findings and define BuTT's role beyond the CR1 setting.

papers.t: Response to venetoclax-containing regimens in patients with relapsed/refractory (R/R) T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (T-ALL) and lymphoblastic lymphoma (T-LBL)
Is Circulating Tumor DNA Ready for Clinical Use in Large B-cell Lymphoma?
papers.c: Circulating tumor DNA detects measurable residual disease (MRD) after therapy which is emerging as an adjunct tool for complex clinical decision-making. We discuss how MRD after therapy can be clinically implemented and additional data needed to unlock its full potential.
ab: Response assessment after frontline therapy for large B-cell lymphoma risk-stratifies patients into those at low risk for relapse and those with residual disease. Positron emission tomography scans form the cornerstone of the response criteria but cannot detect molecular-only disease. Circulating tumor DNA detects measurable residual disease (MRD) after therapy which is emerging as an adjunct tool for complex clinical decision-making. We discuss how MRD after therapy can be clinically implemented and additional data needed to unlock its full potential.

papers.t: Real-world evidence study of brentuximab vedotin retreatment in patients with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in Europe
papers.c: Adverse events including peripheral neuropathy were more common at first treatment. These results suggest that BV retreatment is effective and generally well tolerated for patients with CTCL.
ab: In advanced cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL), allogeneic stem cell transplant is the only curative option, but many patients are ineligible and relapse after systemic therapy, requiring retreatment with prior therapies. Brentuximab vedotin (BV), an anti-CD30 monoclonal antibody drug conjugated with monomethyl auristatin E, is approved by the European Medicines Agency for adult patients with CD30+ CTCL after ≥1 prior systemic therapy. We present efficacy and safety findings of BV retreatment from a multi-center, retrospective real-world study of 26 patients with CTCL conducted in Europe (NCT05886478). Overall response rate was higher after first BV treatment versus BV retreatment (88.5% vs. 54.2%), but progression-free survival was longer after retreatment (9.8 months, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 5.1-11.1) versus first treatment (8.1 months, 95% CI: 6.7-11.0). Adverse events including peripheral neuropathy were more common at first treatment. These results suggest that BV retreatment is effective and generally well tolerated for patients with CTCL.

papers.t: Metabolic tumor volume trajectory during bridging and association with outcomes after CAR T infusion in large B-cell lymphoma
Impact of residual clonal plasma cell proliferation rate after autologous stem cell transplant on outcomes in multiple myeloma
Early Treatment Failure in Patients With Relapsed/Refractory Multiple Myeloma Receiving Bispecific T-Cell Engagers: Development and Validation of the CHARGE Prognostic Index
papers.c: The CHARGE index provides a simplified and externally validated framework for predicting treatment outcomes in patients with RRMM receiving TCEs.
ab: Purpose

Outcomes with bispecific T-cell engagers (TCEs) in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM) are heterogeneous. A practical tool to guide prognosis is needed. We developed a model integrating clinical, biological, and treatment-related variables to predict progression-free survival (PFS) in patients receiving B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA)- or G-protein-coupled receptor class 5 member D-directed TCEs.
Methods

We evaluated outcomes of 577 BCMA-directed and 366 talquetamab treatments across 15 US Multiple Myeloma Immunotherapy Consortium centers. Variables significantly associated with inferior PFS in a multivariate Cox model were incorporated into a prognostic score and validated in an independent multicenter International Myeloma Foundation cohort.
Results

With a median follow-up of 8.4 months, the median PFS was 6.4 months (7.0 months for BCMA TCE; 6.1 months for talquetamab); 92% of patients were triple-class-refractory. Six variables significantly associated with inferior PFS-high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities (HRCAs) [del(17p) or ≥2 HRCAs], hyperferritinemia (≥600 ng/mL), anemia (hemoglobin <9 g/dL), early relapse (<18 months from frontline therapy), general performance status (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status ≥2), and exposure to prior BCMA-directed therapy-were combined to form the CHARGE index, stratifying patients into three risk groups. The median PFS was 21.8 months (95% CI, 11.7 to not reached), 7.1 months (95% CI, 6.1 to 10.1), and 1.6 months (95% CI, 1.2 to 2.5) in the low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups, respectively; hazard ratios (HRs) were 2.0 (95% CI, 1.5 to 2.7) and 4.8 (95% CI, 3.5 to 6.7) for intermediate- and high-risk versus low-risk groups. External validation (n = 173) showed that the median PFS was not reached, 7.0 months, and 3.0 months, with corresponding HRs of 2.9 (95% CI, 1.7 to 4.9) and 4.8 (95% CI, 2.6 to 8.7).
Conclusion
The CHARGE index provides a simplified and externally validated framework for predicting treatment outcomes in patients with RRMM receiving TCEs.

papers.c: ISS stage III, lower HGB, lower ALB, higher CRP, higher M-protein content, lower plateletcrit (PCT) and higher uric acid (UA) were independent predictors of infection (all P < 0.05), and the predictive model performed well, with a model AUC = 0.988, which was significantly better than that of a single indicator; the model was validated by external data in a cohort with AUC = 0.839, which validated the model's predictive efficacy, verifying the generalization ability of the model. The prediction model integrating ISS staging, HGB, ALB, CRP, Monoclonal Protein content, PCT, and UA has excellent discriminatory and calibration abilities, and may provide a reliable tool for risk stratification of infection in MM patients.
ab: To explore the key influencing factors of the risk of nosocomial infection in patients with multiple myeloma (MM), to construct a prediction model to effectively assess the risk of infection, and to provide a basis for individualized infection prevention and control. 245 patients with MM admitted to the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine from 2005 to 2024 were retrospectively included, and the patients' gender, age, BMPC%, time of initial diagnosis, primary symptom at the time of diagnosis, underlying disease, clinical staging (DS staging and ISS staging), treatment regimen, results of bacterial and fungal cultures, and laboratory indexes (e.g., HGB, Rdw%, platelet corpuscular pressure PCT, uric acid, creatinine, β2-MG, CRP, and M protein content). Potential risk factors were screened by univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses, and logistic regression models were constructed in R language and verified for predictive efficacy with external data. ISS stage III, lower HGB, lower ALB, higher CRP, higher M-protein content, lower plateletcrit (PCT) and higher uric acid (UA) were independent predictors of infection (all P < 0.05), and the predictive model performed well, with a model AUC = 0.988, which was significantly better than that of a single indicator; the model was validated by external data in a cohort with AUC = 0.839, which validated the model's predictive efficacy, verifying the generalization ability of the model. The prediction model integrating ISS staging, HGB, ALB, CRP, Monoclonal Protein content, PCT, and UA has excellent discriminatory and calibration abilities, and may provide a reliable tool for risk stratification of infection in MM patients.

papers.t: T cell redirection in high-risk smouldering multiple myeloma: can deep responses prevent progression to multiple myeloma?
Impact of socioeconomic status on treatment and survival in multiple myeloma in Australia
papers.c: These findings demonstrate significant disparities in treatment and outcomes favouring higher SES, independent of biological factors, within a universal healthcare system. This suggests that non-biological factors continue to influence access to standard-of-care therapy and survival, warranting further research to identify and address barriers to equitable care.
ab: Outcomes in multiple myeloma (MM) have improved significantly but remain heterogeneous. We assessed the impact of non-biological social determinants of health on treatment and survival outcomes in Australia using data from the Australian and New Zealand Myeloma and Related Diseases Registry. A total of 4405 patients diagnosed with MM between June 2012 and October 2025 across 44 Australian sites were assigned an area-level socioeconomic status (SES) using individual postcodes. Baseline characteristics, treatment and survival outcomes were compared across high (n = 1484), medium (n = 1463), and low (n = 1458) SES tertiles. Lower neighbourhood SES was associated with higher BMI, poorer functional status, more comorbidities (diabetes, cardiac and pulmonary disease), Asian ethnicity and greater remoteness. Independent of these baseline differences, patients from lower SES neighbourhoods were less likely to receive an autologous stem cell transplant (odds ratio = 1.1 medium vs low, p = 0.41; 1.5 high vs low, p < 0.01) and time to reach ASCT following induction was longer (p < 0.001) despite this being standard-of-care therapy with proven survival benefit. Median overall survival was shorter for the low SES group at 78.5 months compared to 92.5 months (HR = 0.85, p = 0.01) and 86.7 months (HR = 0.85, p = 0.01) for the medium and high SES groups respectively. These findings demonstrate significant disparities in treatment and outcomes favouring higher SES, independent of biological factors, within a universal healthcare system. This suggests that non-biological factors continue to influence access to standard-of-care therapy and survival, warranting further research to identify and address barriers to equitable care.

papers.t: GPRC5D-Directed Antibodies in Multiple Myeloma: New Agents and Frontline Strategies From IMS 2026
Modeling Long-Term Progression-Free Survival in Newly Diagnosed Multiple Myeloma Treated With Daratumumab, Bortezomib, Lenalidomide, and Dexamethasone
papers.c: PFS projections were significantly longer with DVRd than VRd in TE (additional 118 months; 9.8 years) and TIE patients (additional 47 months; 3.9 years) across all seven distributions. These extrapolations reinforce the benefit of DVRd as standard of care in NDMM regardless of transplant eligibility.
ab: Daratumumab, bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone (DVRd) significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) versus VRd in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM) in transplant eligible (TE; PERSEUS) and transplant-ineligible (TIE; CEPHEUS) populations. Median PFS with DVRd has not been reached in either study. This analysis extrapolated PFS data from PERSEUS and CEPHEUS (TIE subgroup) to estimate long-term outcomes for DVRd. Following UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidance on survival data extrapolation, seven parametric distributions were fitted to model PFS data. In PERSEUS (TE population), the projected median PFS range across distributions was 158-255 months versus 76-119 months and best-fit (exponential distribution) PFS estimates were 205 months (17.1 [range, 13.2-21.2] years, DVRd) versus 87 months (7.3 [range, 6.3-9.9] years, VRd). For CEPHEUS (TIE population), projected median PFS range across distributions was 96-118 months versus 52-54 months and best-fit estimates were 100 months (8.3 [range, 8.0-9.8] years, DVRd) versus 53 months (4.4 [range, 4.3-4.5] years, VRd). PFS projections were significantly longer with DVRd than VRd in TE (additional 118 months; 9.8 years) and TIE patients (additional 47 months; 3.9 years) across all seven distributions. These extrapolations reinforce the benefit of DVRd as standard of care in NDMM regardless of transplant eligibility.
